overview: The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth joined two states in 1569 and became a major European power. Its inhabitants built palaces and synagogues, observed the heavens, traded, farmed and debated how government should work. Nobles enjoyed political privileges that most residents did not share. These cards cover the seventeenth-century state and its later, diminished territory, with dated examples of both impressive achievements and ordinary household needs.

periods.title: Union and elected kings
periods.summary: The Union of Lublin created a joint political framework while Lithuania retained institutions of its own.

periods.title: War, rebuilding and scholarship
periods.summary: Cossack revolt and wars with neighboring powers devastated communities. The same era produced major buildings and astronomical publications.

periods.title: Political weakness and new learning
periods.summary: War and foreign intervention constrained the Commonwealth. Intellectual and educational reform gathered momentum during the eighteenth century.

periods.title: Partitions and attempts at reform
periods.summary: Three partitions reduced and finally eliminated the independent state. The Constitution of 1791 attempted major institutional change between those losses.

sections.title: A shared state with unequal freedoms

items.text: The Union of Lublin was concluded on 1 July 1569. A shared parliament linked the Polish Crown and Grand Duchy of Lithuania, while Lithuanian and local assemblies continued. The Commonwealth was a negotiated political union, not simply a new name for one modern nation.
Noblemen elected the monarch after the last Jagiellon king died in 1572. Political rights centered on the nobility, or szlachta. Peasants working under serfdom did not enjoy those same freedoms.

Large estates relied on agricultural labor, including compulsory service from peasants. Grain production connected rural livelihoods with trade. Wars and epidemics could destroy crops, workshops and households, not just change the names on a map.

Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Greek Catholics, Protestants and Jews lived within the Commonwealth’s changing boundaries. Their rights were unequal and changed over time. The existence of several faiths did not guarantee freedom from discrimination.

sections.title: Craft, buildings and observing the heavens

items.text: Jan III Sobieski acquired the Wilanów estate in 1677. Its palace grew from a modest residence into a richly decorated building with separate royal apartments, gardens and a working estate. Surviving decoration presents a ruler interested in art and learning as well as military glory.

The wooden synagogue at Gwoździec, in present-day Ukraine, was built around the middle of the seventeenth century. Paintings and biblical texts covered its interior. Separate spaces accommodated men and women; a later annex also served as a school and a warmer place for winter worship.

Its painted interior was renovated in 1729. The spectacular ceiling seen in POLIN Museum today is a modern reconstruction, made in 2011-2012 using traditional tools and materials. It helps explain lost craftsmanship, but it is not the original timber roof.

In Gdańsk, Johannes Hevelius published detailed lunar observations in Selenographia in 1647. He drew phases and surface features and proposed names for them. Careful description and illustration were important achievements even when later astronomers chose different names.

His 1673 book Machina coelestis illustrated instruments and a rooftop observatory, with Elisabeth Hevelius among those shown working. After her husband’s death, Elisabeth completed the publication of his star research in 1690. Astronomy here was also a family collaboration.

Maria Kazimiera, later queen, adopted a French fashion for receiving visitors while reclining in bed. Letters and diaries record the custom in 1662, before her marriage to Sobieski, and later at court. A formal visit did not always require the hostess to get up. This was elite fashion, not a description of every home.

A letter from 1696 even connects royal family life with the problem of persuading adults to hold a grandchild. The museum’s study uses these personal messages alongside diaries: intimate family concerns can survive in the same archive as affairs of state.

POLIN’s account of eighteenth-century Jewish towns brings markets, taverns, homes and synagogues together. Household life and commerce were closely connected, with women playing important roles in the home. One community’s routines cannot stand in for every town or religious group.

The Commission of National Education began work in 1773 after the suppression of the Jesuit order disrupted schooling. Reformers reorganized schools, planned teacher training and expanded lessons in Polish and the sciences, including physics and geometry. New curricula did not mean equal schooling for every child.

The Society for Elementary Books, founded in 1775, prepared textbooks and syllabuses. Some of those books remained in use during the nineteenth century. Educational reform meant practical work on what teachers and pupils would actually read.

Around the middle of the seventeenth century, Adam Kazanowski’s Warsaw palace had a two-room bath with tubs and a controlled supply of steam. The furnace stood outside the bathing rooms, possibly below them. That last detail is an interpretation, not a securely observed floor plan.

Bathhouses could combine washing with socializing and services such as shaving, cupping or tooth extraction. The museum study describes varied buildings and customers. These historical treatments tell us what was offered, not whether it was safe or effective.

Seventeenth- and eighteenth-century noble household inventories list basins, pitchers, combs and shaving equipment. Richer households could display silver fittings. Researchers must also allow for increasingly detailed inventories: more entries on paper do not automatically mean a sudden invention of cleanliness.

Eighteenth-century inventories also mention copper chamber pots kept under beds; the wealthiest could own silver ones. A fancy material did not give the pot a fancy job. These were possessions of particular households, not proof that everyone had the same toilet arrangements.

In early-modern Gdańsk, latrines commonly stood at the back of town plots. Excavations preserve timber linings of pits, while the buildings above them are often missing. Archaeologists therefore combine remains with pictures and written descriptions when reconstructing the whole structure.

Those pits also collected discarded objects and organic waste. Studying their contents can reveal food and living conditions. Yesterday’s rubbish can become tomorrow’s historical evidence, although an object in a cesspit does not by itself explain why it ended up there.

Gdańsk’s pharmacies were supervised by a city physician and civic officials. In 1665, Johann Ernst Scheffler and Johan Fabritius produced the Dispensatorium Gedanense, an official list of medicines. This records efforts to organize pharmacy practice; a medicine’s inclusion does not prove that it worked.

sections.title: A short sample of written language

items.text: On the façade of Wilanów Palace, the Latin inscription “REFULSIT SOL IN CLYPEIS” means “the sun shone on the shields.” It belongs to the imagery of Sobieski’s late-seventeenth-century residence and adapts a biblical phrase. This is a real architectural inscription, not a phrase invented for this card.

The shields also recalled the Sobieski family’s emblem. The museum’s art-historical study interprets the decoration as a statement about royal authority. Latin served this learned public message; it was not the everyday language of all the Commonwealth’s residents.

Russia, Prussia and Austria took territory in the first partition of 1772. The Commonwealth survived with reduced territory. Its later appearance under the map label “Poland” refers to this remaining state, not a new country founded in 1783.

The Constitution of 3 May 1791 separated branches of government and abolished the liberum veto, which had allowed a deputy to obstruct parliamentary proceedings. Its text survives in manuscripts and contemporary printed editions. Constitutional design is a documented achievement, even though its implementation was cut short.

Article IV placed peasants under the protection of law and government, but also preserved obligations arising from agreements with landowners. It did not abolish serfdom. The distinction matters: a promise of protection was not the same as equal freedom.

Russia and Prussia carried out the second partition in 1793. The uprising led by Tadeusz Kościuszko in 1794 was defeated. Russia, Prussia and Austria divided the remaining territory in 1795, ending the Commonwealth’s independent institutions.

Partition changed people’s rulers rather than making communities disappear. Jewish residents, for example, came under Austrian, Prussian or Russian government, with new laws shaping daily life. The histories of the Commonwealth’s inhabitants continued beyond the state’s ending.

ending.text: The third partition in 1795 divided the Commonwealth’s remaining territory among Russia, Prussia and Austria. Independent government ended; its diverse communities continued under new rulers. The imported endpoint of 1800 for the later map record has therefore been corrected to 1795.
